title: Sewer air test times: how long to hold for a 1.0 psi drop (or 0.5 psi), 4 to 15 inch (ASTM F1417)
text: Minimum time for a 1.0 psi drop on a low-pressure air test of plastic gravity sewer (ASTM F1417 / UNI-B-6 table, Q = 0.0015): 4 in 3:46 up to 597 ft; 6 in 5:40 up to 398 ft; 8 in 7:34 up to 298 ft; 10 in 9:26 up to 239 ft; 12 in 11:20 up to 199 ft; 15 in 14:10 up to 159 ft. Longer runs, in seconds with L in feet: 0.380 x L (4 in), 0.854 x L (6 in), 1.520 x L (8 in), 2.374 x L (10 in), 3.418 x L (12 in), 5.342 x L (15 in). Example: 300 ft of 8 in = 1.520 x 300 = 456 seconds = 7:36. If the spec times a 0.5 psi drop instead, every time is half (8 in: 3:47 up to 298 ft, then 0.760 x L). Procedure in these specs: pressurize to 4.0 psi above the groundwater back pressure (never over 9 psi), let it settle, start timing at 3.5 psi; the line passes if it takes longer than the table time to lose the drop. Never stand in front of a plug under pressure. The job spec's own table governs.
source: ASTM F1417 / UNI-B-6 times as printed in Berkeley County Water & Sanitation Section 02731 (Rev 4/2023), Table 1 (1.0 psig) and Table 2 (0.5 psig); same 1.0 psi times in American Water spec 33 01 30.13 Table 2 (rev. Jan 2017)
note: Replaces test-2 in place: test-2 printed the 0.5 psig table (3:47, 0.760 L for 8 in) as the 1.0 psig times. Greenbook air test numbers stay in gb-5.

title: Mandrel size for PVC sewer pipe: SDR 35 and SDR 26, 6 to 15 inch, at 5 and 7.5 percent deflection
text: A deflection mandrel is the pipe's base inside diameter times 0.95 for a 5 percent test or 0.925 for 7.5 percent. SDR 35 (ASTM D3034) as printed in county mandrel tables, base ID then 5 and 7.5 percent mandrel, inches: 6 in 5.742, 5.454, 5.31; 8 in 7.665, 7.281, 7.09; 10 in 9.563, 9.084, 8.84; 12 in 11.361, 10.792, 10.51; 15 in 13.898, 7.5 percent 12.86 (the printed 5 percent figure, 13.023, is not 95 percent of 13.898, so it is not confirmed). SDR 26 (D3034), 5 percent: 6 in 5.33, 8 in 7.11, 10 in 8.87, 12 in 10.55, 15 in 12.90; 7.5 percent: 5.19, 6.93, 8.64, 10.27, 12.56. Some specs size the mandrel from the average inside diameter instead, which gives a bigger mandrel, so use the table in your spec. C900 pressure pipe has its own sizes. The inspector proves the mandrel with its ring before the pull.
source: ASTM D3034 mandrel tables as printed in Fulton County standard detail 106, Table 105-1 (SDR 35 values; same 7.5 percent column as Miami-Dade WASD UC-350 3.02-E for SDR 35) and Berkeley County Water & Sanitation mandrel sizes table (D3034 SDR 26)
edition: Fulton County detail 106 (page dated 2026-02-18); Miami-Dade UC-350 (1/1999); Berkeley County mandrel table (undated)
note: Fulton table 105-1 does not print "SDR 35"; its base IDs (8 in 7.665) and 7.5 percent column equal Miami-Dade UC-350 SDR 35 table, and its 8 in 5 percent value (7.281) matches the Greenbook SDR 35 example (gb-6, 7.282). American Water 33 01 30.13 Table 4 sizes from average ID (8 in SDR 26 7.329).

title: How much cover over a water main (how deep to bury it): who sets the number and how it is measured
topic: Water mains: cover and bury depth
text: No federal rule sets the cover over a water main: the plans, the water agency's standard details or the state's drinking water rules set it, mainly to keep the pipe below frost and away from traffic loads. The Ten States Recommended Standards for Water Works (2018, Section 8.7.3), which many state programs follow, gives no number: mains are to be covered with enough earth or other insulation to prevent freezing. Cover is measured from the top of the pipe to finished grade, not from the trench bottom. Check the plan profile and the agency standard for the minimum, and for what to do where it cannot be met (insulation, a deeper line, or an engineer's detail). Cover is a different number from the 5 ft trench protection depth: cover is how deep the pipe is buried; protection is about the trench walls.
source: Recommended Standards for Water Works (Ten States Standards), 2018 edition, Section 8.7.3 Cover (our summary); top of pipe to finish grade as defined in state rules such as 327 IAC 8-3.2-17(d)

title: Oregon water main cover: at least 30 inches over distribution piping (OAR 333-061-0050)
topic: Water mains: cover and bury depth
text: Oregon's drinking water construction standards require distribution piping to be bedded in material free from rocks and to have a cover of at least 30 inches (OAR 333-061-0050(8)(f)). A main laid under a stream or other watercourse also gets at least 30 inches of cover over the pipe (333-061-0050(9)(d)). These are the state minimums for public water systems; the water agency's standard or the plans can require more for frost or traffic, and the deeper number governs. Cover is measured from the top of the pipe to finished grade. It is not a trench safety number: protecting the trench walls is a separate Oregon OSHA rule.
source: OAR 333-061-0050(8)(f) and (9)(d), Construction Standards (amended PH 7-2023, effective 2023-02-01)

title: Indiana water main cover: 36 to 60 inches depending on the county (327 IAC 8-3.2-17)
topic: Water mains: cover and bury depth
text: Indiana's public water system rule requires earthen cover over water mains as set by county in the table in 327 IAC 8-3.2-17(d); the table runs from 36 inches to 60 inches, and the cover is measured from the top of the pipe to the proposed finish grade. Look up the job's county in that table: the county-by-county values were not copied into this card, so the exact number for a given county is not confirmed here. The water utility's standard or the plans can require more, and the deeper number governs.
source: 327 IAC 8-3.2-17(d), Installation, cover table and footnote 1 (Indiana Administrative Code, current through 2025-06-25)

title: Utah water main cover: enough to prevent freezing, no set depth in the state rule (R309-550-8)
topic: Water mains: cover and bury depth
text: Utah's drinking water rule requires all water mains to be covered with sufficient earth or other insulation to prevent freezing (Utah Admin. Code R309-550-8(5)); it sets no depth in inches. The exception is a noncommunity system that is shut down and drained when temperatures are below freezing. Under a water crossing the rule calls for at least 2 ft of cover, or more as local conditions require (R309-550-8(8)(b)(i)). The depth for a job comes from the plans and the water agency's standard. Cover is measured from the top of the pipe to finished grade.
source: Utah Admin. Code R309-550-8(5) Burial Cover and (8)(b)(i) (amended Utah State Bulletin 2014-23, effective 2014-11-10)

title: Virginia water main cover: enough earth to prevent freezing, no set depth in the state rule (12VAC5-590-1220)
topic: Water mains: cover and bury depth
text: Virginia's Waterworks Regulations require all buried distribution pipe to have sufficient earth or other suitable cover, or encasement, to prevent freezing and protect it from external forces (12VAC5-590-1220, Pipe cover). The rule sets no depth in inches, so the depth for a job comes from the plans and the water utility's standard. Cover is measured from the top of the pipe to finished grade.
source: 12VAC5-590-1220 Pipe cover (amended Virginia Register Vol. 37 Issue 20, effective 2021-06-23)

title: Sewer smells like rotten eggs or sewer gas in a manhole, wet well or new sewer: hydrogen sulfide, stay out and test
text: A rotten egg or sewer gas smell in a manhole, wet well, lift station or sewer line is usually hydrogen sulfide (H2S), not a gas line. Stay out and keep heads out of the opening; test the air from outside with a calibrated 4-gas meter before anyone enters, and ventilate. Your nose is no warning: OSHA lists loss of smell at about 100 to 150 ppm, and NIOSH's immediately dangerous level is 100 ppm. The federal construction limit is 10 ppm averaged over 8 hours (29 CFR 1926.55). A manhole or wet well is a confined space, so entry follows 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA: testing, ventilation, an attendant and rescue planned. If someone is down or not answering, do not go in after them: call 911. A natural gas smell at a gas line or meter, not in a sewer, is a gas leak: get out, upwind, and call 911 and the gas company.
source: OSHA Hydrogen Sulfide pages: Standards (29 CFR 1926.55, 10 ppm TWA; NIOSH IDLH 100 ppm) and Hazards (loss of smell at 100-150 ppm); 29 CFR 1926.1200-1213 (Subpart AA)
edition: OSHA web pages as read 2026-11-22; 29 CFR 1926, eCFR current 2026
note: Pairs with the instant-emergency fix the review asks for (emergency.ts / app): today the sewer-smell questions never reach Ask.

title: Thrust block soil bearing: which psf number to use when the tables disagree (sand 2,000 or 4,000)
topic: Water mains: thrust blocks and restraint
text: Block bearing area = thrust divided by the allowable soil bearing, so the soil value sets the block size. Use the value on the plans' thrust block detail or in the geotechnical report first. Published tables disagree: DIPRA's guide (Table 8, a guide for about 4 ft deep) lists sand 4,000 lb per sq ft, soft clay 1,000, silt 1,500, sandy silt 3,000, sandy clay 6,000, hard clay 9,000, muck 0; a DOT thrust blocking standard (RD250, Table B) lists sand 2,000, sand and gravel 3,000, soft clay 1,000, muck or peat 0. Example: an 8 in C900 90 degree bend at 150 psi pushes about 13,646 lb, so 6.8 sq ft at 2,000 psf but 3.4 sq ft at 4,000. With no plan value, ask the engineer; the lower value gives the bigger, safer block. Size for test pressure and pour against undisturbed soil. Say which soil value the size uses.
source: DIPRA Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe, rev. May 2015, Table 8 (p. 71); ODOT standard drawing RD250 Thrust Blocking, Table B (2024 standard drawings)
edition: DIPRA guide rev. May 2015; RD250 in the 2024 standard drawings
note: Both tables were read as extracted text with soils and values matched in order (the PDF columns are not aligned), hence medium.

title: Water main hydrostatic (pressure) test: test pressure, how long to hold, allowed make-up water (AWWA C600 / C605)
text: Ductile iron (AWWA C600, per DIPRA's guide) and PVC (AWWA C605 Sec. 9.3.5) water mains are tested at no less than 1.5 times the working pressure at the lowest point of the section; C605 also requires at least 1.25 times the working pressure at the highest point. Never test above the rating of the pipe, fittings, valves or thrust restraint. Hold the test 2 hours. Example: 150 psi working means a 225 psi test at the low point. Pump in only enough water to hold pressure and measure it: allowed make-up water L (gallons per hour) = S x D x square root of P / 148,000, with S = feet tested, D = nominal diameter in inches, P = average test pressure in psi; 1,000 ft of 8 in at 150 psi allows about 0.66 gal/hr. Fill slowly and bleed the air first; pressure that keeps sagging usually means air, a passing valve or a leak. The job spec and water agency set the test pressure and time, and they govern.
source: DIPRA Installation Guide (rev. May 2015) Sec. 7.2, p. 81 (1.5 times at the lowest point, 2 hours); Uni-Bell brief on PVC field test pressure (2025-09-09) quoting AWWA C605 Sec. 9.3.5; allowance formula as in county test specs (testing-water-2)
note: Replaces test-1 in place (it said "Greenbook: 4 hours" and "Greenbook working plus 50 psi" on every job; those stay in gb-7). Formula carried from testing-water-2 (county spec, not re-read today); 0.66 gal/hr arithmetic checked.

text: Testing a new ductile iron water main, summarized from the DIPRA Installation Guide (revised May 2015), which follows AWWA C600 and C651. Pressure test: at least 1.5 times the working pressure at the lowest point of the section, held for at least 2 hours (150 psi working means a 225 psi test). Measure the make-up water needed to hold pressure; examples of the testing allowance at 150 psi are about 0.50 gallon per hour per 1,000 feet of 6 inch and 0.99 for 12 inch. Brace or restrain temporary plugs and caps. Flush at 3.0 feet per second: about 260 gpm for a 6 inch main and 1,060 gpm for a 12 inch (Table 9). Chlorination (AWWA C651): tablet method, granules at the start and every 500 feet and 5-gram tablets at joints, fill slowly at 1 foot per second or less, hold 24 hours (48 hours if the water is colder than 41 F), about 25 mg/L; continuous feed, at least 25 mg/L going in and at least 10 mg/L left after 24 hours; slug method, at least 100 mg/L for at least 3 hours, start over if it drops below 50 mg/L. Flush the strong chlorine out within about a day, dechlorinate where the discharge rule requires it, then take bacteria samples. The water agency's spec governs.
title: Water main pressure test, flushing and chlorination basics (DIPRA guide, AWWA C600 and C651)
topic: Spec books: pipe testing and inspection (air, water, mandrel, video)
source: Ductile Iron Pipe Research Association (DIPRA), Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe, revised May 2015, hosted by McWane (our summary; read 2026-11-20)
note: 6 inch flushing flow was 400 gpm; DIPRA Table 9 (p. 79) says 260 gpm at 3.0 ft/s (and 1,060 for 12 inch). 260 = 6 in area x 3 ft/s.

text: Thrust restraint basics, summarized from the DIPRA Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe (revised May 2015). Water pressure pushes on every bend, tee, reducer, valve and dead end. Example thrust at 100 psi: a 12 inch 90 degree bend pushes about 19,353 lb and a 12 inch dead end about 13,685 lb; thrust scales straight with pressure, so use test pressure, not working pressure. Example soil bearing values at 4 feet deep (Table 8): muck 0, sand about 4,000 lb per square foot, hard clay about 9,000; agency thrust block tables can list sand lower (2,000), and the plans' or geotech value governs. Common practice is block bearing area = thrust divided by the allowable soil bearing, poured against undisturbed soil. Blocks are concrete of at least 2,000 psi, cured at least five days before testing. Mechanical joints by themselves hold no thrust. Restrained joints (or wedge-action glands) are used instead of blocks where space is tight or the soil behind the block may be dug out later; the restrained length comes from the engineer or the agency table. Always build what the plans or the agency thrust block detail shows; these numbers are examples, not a design.
title: Thrust blocks at bends and dead ends: forces, soil bearing values, how strong the concrete (DIPRA guide)
source: Ductile Iron Pipe Research Association (DIPRA), Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe, revised May 2015, hosted by McWane (our summary; read 2026-11-20)
